Did fertiliser price changes go with later wheat price changes?

World Bank monthly commodity prices, from 2015 to the latest month available

Shruti Singla

11 November 2026

  • 1. Question
  • 2. Data
  • 3. Method

1. Question

Fertiliser is a major cost of growing wheat. Did monthly changes in fertiliser prices (DAP and urea) go together with later monthly changes in wheat prices, and over what delay? I use the 2021 to 2022 fertiliser price spike as a natural episode to look at, but the models use the whole sample.

This is a descriptive time-series study. It measures association and predictive order, not proven cause and effect.

2. Data

  • Source: World Bank, Commodity Markets (“Pink Sheet”), monthly prices in nominal US dollars. File status: Updated on November 03, 2026.
  • Sample: January 2015 to October 2026 (142 months). Thirteen earlier months are used only to build lagged values.
  • Series used:
Series Column in World Bank file Unit
Wheat (US HRW) Wheat, US HRW ($/mt)
DAP DAP ($/mt)
Urea Urea ($/mt)
Crude oil (average) Crude oil, average ($/bbl)
Natural gas (Europe) Natural gas, Europe ($/mmbtu)

Cleaning and checks (full list in output/tables/data_validation.csv): the date column was parsed from the World Bank format (for example 2021M06); the placeholder for missing values was converted to missing; the monthly sequence was checked for gaps and duplicates; prices were checked to be positive; one-month moves larger than 25% were flagged for inspection (output/tables/outlier_flags.csv) but not removed, because they correspond to genuine market swings rather than errors.

3. Method

  1. Monthly log changes. Price levels trend and wander, so regressing one level on another can look significant by accident. I work with monthly log changes (roughly monthly percentage changes). Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests below: a small p-value supports stationarity (the p-values from this test are bounded between 0.01 and 0.99).
Series Transformation n ADF statistic p-value
Wheat (US HRW) log price (level) 142 -1.854 0.637
DAP log price (level) 142 -2.737 0.269
Urea log price (level) 142 -2.641 0.310
Wheat (US HRW) monthly log change 142 -3.904 0.016
DAP monthly log change 142 -3.429 0.053
Urea monthly log change 142 -5.021 0.010

Note: for DAP the test does not reject a unit root at the 5% level (p = 0.053), so stationarity of its monthly changes is borderline.

  1. Lead-lag correlations between wheat now and fertiliser k months earlier.
  2. Distributed-lag regression (main model, window fixed in advance: months 0 to 6). Wheat change on fertiliser change today and in the previous 6 months, plus lagged changes in crude oil and European natural gas as controls. Standard errors are Newey-West (HAC) because monthly price changes are usually autocorrelated. The cumulative association is the sum of the lag coefficients.
  3. Granger-type tests in both directions, because high wheat prices could also pull fertiliser prices up.
  4. Robustness and sensitivity: other lag lengths, with and without energy controls, two targeted sensitivity checks, and three sub-periods. A 12-month window is shown separately as exploratory, because it was added after the main results were seen.

4. Findings

4.1 Prices over time

4.2 Main estimates

Both variables are in logs, so a coefficient reads as a percentage response. The cumulative association is the total across the window: it says by how many percent wheat prices are higher (or lower) by the end of the window, in association with a one-off 1% rise in the fertiliser price.

  • DAP: cumulative association over months 0-6 = 0.40 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.78; n = 142). In words: a one-off 1% rise in the price goes with wheat prices about 0.4% higher by the end of the window. The interval excludes zero, so the estimate is distinguishable from zero at the 5% level. Adjusted R-squared of the model: 0.04.
  • Urea: cumulative association over months 0-6 = 0.41 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.65; n = 142). In words: a one-off 1% rise in the price goes with wheat prices about 0.4% higher by the end of the window. The interval excludes zero, so the estimate is distinguishable from zero at the 5% level. Adjusted R-squared of the model: 0.10.

Low R-squared values mean that most month-to-month movement in wheat prices is not explained by fertiliser and energy price changes.

4.3 Timing: which delays matter?

Exploratory, added after seeing the main results: the same model with a 12-month window, to check what happens beyond month 6.

4.4 Does the direction matter? (Granger-type tests)

Small p-values mean past values of the first series help predict the second. They show predictive order, not causation. Twenty-four tests are run here, so with a 5% threshold one or two would be expected to look significant by chance alone (a strict Bonferroni cut-off would be about 0.002).

5. Limitations

  • Nominal prices. No inflation or exchange-rate adjustment. A general commodity boom or a dollar move can lift all prices together.
  • Benchmark export prices, not farm prices. These are World Bank benchmark quotes, not what farmers pay or receive in any one country. The file’s Description sheet defines them as: wheat, US hard red winter (No. 2, Gulf export price; No. 1 ordinary protein up to June 2020); DAP, spot f.o.b. US Gulf; urea (Ukraine, prill), spot f.o.b. Black Sea until February 2022 and f.o.b. Middle East from March 2022.
  • Series definitions change inside the sample. The urea quotation point changed in March 2022, in the middle of the shock window; I test this in section 4.5. The wheat benchmark grade changed around mid-2020. The European gas control switches from an import border price to the Dutch TTF price from April 2015, shortly after the sample starts.
  • Common shocks. Energy prices affect both fertiliser and wheat; I control for oil and gas. Events such as the 2022 war in Ukraine plausibly hit both markets at once and are not separately controlled. The data also show a joint jump in oil, gas and urea in March 2026; section 4.5 shows what happens when the sample ends before 2026. I have not investigated its cause.
  • Short sub-samples. The shock-window estimates rest on few months, so they cannot say whether the relationship changed.
  • Association only. Regressions with lags and Granger-type tests show timing, not proven cause. Many tests were run, so isolated “significant” results should not be over-read.
  • The 12-month window is exploratory. It was added after the main results were seen and should not be treated as a pre-planned test.

6. Interpretation

Bottom line. Between January 2015 and October 2026, rises in fertiliser prices went with higher wheat prices about five to six months later. The evidence is clearer for urea than for DAP, the effect is modest, and it is an association, not proof of cause.

  • Size. Over the pre-set six-month window the cumulative association is 0.41 for urea (95% CI 0.17 to 0.65) and 0.40 for DAP (0.02 to 0.78). In words: a one-off 1% rise in the fertiliser price goes with wheat prices roughly 0.4% higher by the end of the window. The models explain little of wheat’s month-to-month movement (adjusted R-squared 0.10 for urea, 0.04 for DAP).
  • Timing. The association sits at months 5 and 6. Correlations peak there (urea 0.25 and 0.27; DAP 0.24 at month 6, and also 0.20 in the same month), and the exploratory 12-month model shows nothing beyond month 6. Months 1 to 3 show little. That is why the urea models restricted to months 0 to 3 are not significant, and why the rolling chart, which uses months 1 to 3 (a window set before the data were examined), hovers near zero. It does not contradict the main finding.
  • Urea is more convincing than DAP. Urea stays significant when the sample ends in December 2025 (0.32, CI 0.08 to 0.57), when the March 2022 benchmark change is set to missing (0.29, CI 0.07 to 0.51), and in the 12-month model. Its six-lag Granger test is significant (p = 0.002). DAP is fragile: its interval only just excludes zero, it is not significant in the 0 to 3 or 0 to 12 month models with energy controls, and its Granger tests show nothing (smallest p = 0.19). Without energy controls DAP is significant at all three window lengths, which suggests part of its apparent link may run through energy prices.
  • Direction. Wheat prices do not help predict later fertiliser prices at any lag tested (smallest p = 0.17), which fits fertiliser leading wheat rather than following it.
  • What I cannot say. The 2021 to 2022 window has too few months to tell whether the relationship changed: every sub-period interval includes zero. I cannot rule out common shocks that moved both prices, such as the 2022 war in Ukraine or the general commodity cycle; only oil and gas are controlled for. I have not tested why the delay is about six months.

7. Reproducibility

  • File: CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx (sheet “Monthly Prices”)
  • File status: “Updated on November 03, 2026” (stated inside the file)
  • Obtained: downloaded from the World Bank website by the project author
